content: Interactive Voice Response (IVR) in telephony is a technology that enables a computer to recognize voice and touch-tone inputs during a standard phone call. The IVR system can respond to callers with either pre-recorded or dynamically generated audio messages, guiding them on how to proceed further. These systems are capable of managing a wide range of functions by breaking down the interface into a series of simple menu options. Once implemented, IVR systems are highly scalable and can handle large volumes of calls efficiently. For example, when a caller dials a phone number connected to an IVR system, the system executes an application associated with the dialed number, known as Dialed Number Information Service (DNIS). The application uses pre-recorded audio files or dynamically generated Text-to-Speech (TTS) audio to present the caller with available options. The caller can then make selections using either Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency (DTMF) tones or spoken commands. Speech recognition technology is often employed to facilitate more complex transactions and streamline the menu structure. IVR systems are commonly used to manage high call volumes, reduce operational costs, and enhance customer experience. Typical applications include telephone banking, televoting, and credit card transactions. Large organizations often use IVR to extend their business hours and provide services that align with the customer experience offered through web interfaces. The widespread use of mobile phones has made voice services more accessible and convenient, leading to increased adoption of IVR systems. Call centers utilize IVR systems to identify and segment callers, enabling personalized services based on customer profiles. Callers can choose between automated services, waiting in a queue, or requesting a callback at a convenient time. By integrating Computer Telephony Integration (CTI), IVR systems can access network databases to identify callers using Calling Line Identification (CLI). This method is accurate for approximately 80% of inbound calls and is expected to improve as mobile phone usage increases. In cases where CLI is unavailable, callers may be asked to verify their identity using alternative methods such as a PIN or password. DNIS ensures that the correct application and language are executed by the IVR system. Voice-activated IVR systems, also known as Voice Activated Dialers (VAD), are increasingly replacing traditional switchboard or Private Automatic Branch Exchange (PABX) operators in hospitals and large businesses. These systems reduce caller wait times and allow external callers to page hospital staff or transfer calls directly to the intended recipient. IVR systems are also widely used in entertainment and information services, handling large call spikes for services like mobile content orders, weather forecasts, crossword answers, and adult entertainment. IVR systems provide anonymous access to information, which is particularly useful in healthcare settings. Hospitals and clinics use IVR to deliver test results while preserving patient privacy and avoiding potential embarrassment associated with sensitive information. In clinical trials, pharmaceutical companies use IVR systems to manage large volumes of data and conduct global studies. These systems, often referred to as Voiceform applications, allow callers to respond to questions in their preferred language, with responses logged into a database and potentially recorded for verification. Applications include patient randomization and drug supply management. IVR systems interpret caller responses to voice prompts using DTMF signals or natural language speech recognition. Advanced technologies like Text-to-Speech (TTS) enable IVR systems to deliver complex and dynamic information, such as emails, news reports, or weather updates, in a synthesized voice that closely resembles natural human speech. IVR systems can be deployed in various ways, including on-premises equipment, installations within the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN), or through application service providers (ASP). Common business applications include telephone banking, order placement, caller identification and routing, balance inquiries, and airline ticket booking. Unlike simple voicemail systems, which facilitate person-to-person communication, IVR systems enable person-to-computer interactions. IVR voice forms can enhance the voicemail experience by allowing callers to edit, forward, or delete recorded messages. Automatic Call Distributors (ACD) often serve as the initial point of contact for large businesses, routing calls without requiring input from the caller. In contrast, IVR systems can request input from callers to route calls to specific skill sets, which are groups of call center agents with specialized expertise. Modern IVR applications are designed using languages like VoiceXML, SALT, or T-XML, which resemble the structure of web pages. This approach allows developers to focus on call flow rather than specialized programming. However, creating an effective IVR system requires an understanding of human interaction with the application dialogue to ensure a positive user experience. High-level development tools have simplified the application development process, enabling developers to create call flow diagrams using graphical user interfaces (GUI) and automatically generate application code. These tools also support software integration through mechanisms like HTTP interfaces for websites and Java interfaces for database connections. In telecommunications, an Audio Response Unit (ARU) is a device that provides synthesized voice responses to touch-tone inputs (DTMF) by processing calls based on caller input, database information, or details from the incoming call, such as the time of day. ARUs enhance the number of information calls handled and ensure consistent quality in information retrieval. Despite its advantages, IVR technology is often criticized for being unhelpful and difficult to use due to poor design and a lack of consideration for caller needs. Some callers prefer speaking with a human representative rather than interacting with an automated system. A well-designed IVR system should address caller needs promptly and with minimal complexity, avoiding the frustration commonly referred to as IVR hell.
